title: 7 Best Benchtop Planers in 2026: Straight Knife vs Helical
keywords: which planer is better, knives or helical
description: The DEWALT DW735X is the best benchtop planer for most shops: 13 in capacity and two feed speeds. Seven picks, including helical and quiet models.
dek: The DEWALT DW735X is the best benchtop planer for most shops: 13 in capacity and two feed speeds.
intro: The best benchtop planer for most home shops is the DEWALT DW735X: it handles boards 13 inches wide and 6 inches thick, has two feed speeds for fast stock removal and a clean final pass, and the X kit includes infeed and outfeed tables to fight snipe. If you want a helical head for figured or reclaimed wood, the WEN PL1326 is the value pick, and the Makita 2012NB is the quietest straight-knife machine here.

A thickness planer lets you buy rough lumber for less, bring reclaimed boards back to life and hit an exact thickness. It does one job: it makes the top face parallel to the bottom face. It does not flatten a warped board, and most disappointment with planers comes from expecting it to. Below are seven machines, then the questions buyers ask about cutterheads, snipe, dust and milling.
quickAnswer: Buy the DEWALT DW735X if you want one planer that does everything well. Choose the WEN PL1326 or Cutech 40200H-CT for a helical head on a budget, the Makita 2012NB if noise matters, and the DEWALT DW734 for occasional use. Take light passes of 1/32 to 1/16 inch, connect dust collection, and leave parts long so you can trim off snipe.

blocks.p: The DW735X earns the top spot on its two-speed gearbox, chip ejection and included tables. If you work mostly with figured maple, curly cherry or barn boards, a helical head will reduce tear-out and survive hidden metal better.
Every benchtop planer here handles 12 to 13 inches, which covers nearly all furniture parts. Wider panels are glued up from narrower boards anyway.

sections.h: The 7 Best Benchtop Planers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: Picks are ranked on manufacturer specs for width and thickness capacity, cutterhead type and speed, cuts per inch, motor rating and snipe control, plus warranty, parts availability and recurring owner feedback. No hands-on trials are claimed.

The DW735X is the benchtop planer woodworkers recommend first, and its spec sheet shows why. It surfaces boards up to 13 inches wide and 6 inches thick with a three-knife cutterhead that DeWalt lists at 10,000 RPM. A two-speed gearbox gives you a fast feed for hogging stock down and a slower feed with more cuts per inch for a cleaner last pass.

A fan-assisted chip ejection system blasts chips out through the dust port, which keeps them from being pressed back into the board as dents. The X kit adds infeed and outfeed tables and a spare set of knives; the tables matter because they reduce snipe. The knives are double-sided and disposable, and swapping them is simple. The downsides are weight, noise and how hard it throws chips: without a dust collector or a large separator on a shop vac, the shop gets buried. For most home shops it is still the benchmark machine.
**Pros:** Two feed speeds; 13 in wide by 6 in thick capacity; fan-assisted chip ejection; X kit adds tables and spare knives.
**Cons:** Heavy to lift onto a bench; very loud; throws chips hard without collection.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DEWALT+DW735X+planer&tag=sktiger-20)

The WEN PL1326 puts a helical, or spiral, cutterhead on a machine priced close to straight-knife planers. In place of long knives, the head carries rows of small square inserts set in a spiral. Each insert can be turned to a fresh edge when it dulls or chips, so a hidden nail costs you one insert rather than a full knife set.

The shearing cut of a spiral head generally leaves less tear-out on figured, curly and interlocked grain, and it runs quieter than straight knives. Capacity is 13 inches wide. Owners commonly call it strong value while noting that the tables and overall fit and finish are less refined than premium machines, so checking table alignment at setup is worth the time. If you plane a lot of figured hardwood or reclaimed lumber, it is the best benchtop helical planer for the money on this list.
**Pros:** Spiral head reduces tear-out; inserts rotate individually; quieter than straight knives; low cost for a helical machine.
**Cons:** Fit and finish below premium brands; tables may need aligning; single feed speed.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=WEN+PL1326+helical+planer&tag=sktiger-20)

The Makita 2012NB is the planer for shops where noise matters, such as a garage under a bedroom or a basement in a shared house. Makita lists its operating noise at about 83 decibels, noticeably lower than many benchtop planers, though hearing protection is still a good idea.

It handles boards up to 12 inches wide and roughly 6 inches thick with a two-knife cutterhead. Its Interna-Lok system clamps the cutterhead carriage automatically during the cut to reduce snipe. It is lighter than the DeWalt, which makes it easier to store under a bench and lift into place. The trade-offs are the narrower 12-inch capacity and a single feed rate with fewer cuts per inch than the DW735's finishing speed, so a scraper or sander pass may be needed on demanding work. For quiet, reliable dimensioning of typical furniture stock, owners rate it highly.
**Pros:** Among the quietest by listed noise level; automatic head clamping; lighter and easy to store; proven design.
**Cons:** 12 in width capacity; single feed speed; fewer cuts per inch than the DW735 finish setting.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Makita+2012NB+planer&tag=sktiger-20)

The DW734 is DeWalt's simpler, cheaper planer, and it remains a smart buy for occasional users. It surfaces boards up to 12-1/2 inches wide and 6 inches thick with a three-knife cutterhead DeWalt lists at 10,000 RPM and a single feed rate. A carriage lock helps limit snipe, and the knives are the same double-sided disposable type used on the DW735.

It lacks the DW735's second speed and fan-assisted ejection, so the finish on difficult grain is not quite as fine and chip removal depends more on your vac or collector. It is smaller and lighter, which helps if the planer lives on a shelf between projects. For a hobbyist who mills a few boards a month, it delivers most of the DW735's results for less, with the same DeWalt parts support.
**Pros:** Lower cost than the DW735; three-knife head; carriage lock; compact for storage.
**Cons:** Single speed; no fan-assisted chip ejection; slightly narrower capacity.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DEWALT+DW734+planer&tag=sktiger-20)

The Cutech 40200H-CT is a lighter spiral-head planer built for shops where the planer gets carried to the bench when needed. Its cutterhead uses small indexable inserts, so like other helical machines it tends to leave less tear-out on figured wood and lets you rotate individual inserts after damage. Check the listing for insert material, since Cutech has sold versions with different inserts, and carbide lasts much longer between rotations.

It handles boards up to 13 inches wide. Owners commonly praise the cut quality for the price and the low weight, while noting that the feed rollers and tables are less robust than heavier machines and that minor snipe needs managing with supports or a sacrificial board. It suits a woodworker who mostly planes hardwood for furniture, wants a helical finish and has limited space.
**Pros:** Spiral cutterhead for clean cuts; lighter than most 13 in machines; inserts rotate individually; good finish for the cost.
**Cons:** Lighter build is less robust; snipe needs managing; insert material varies by version.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Cutech+40200H-CT+spiral+planer&tag=sktiger-20)

The Delta 22-555 is built around stability. Its cutterhead carriage rides on four columns and can be locked in place, a design meant to stop the head from rocking as boards enter and leave, which is the main source of snipe. It handles boards up to 13 inches wide and takes reversible knives.

For woodworkers frustrated by snipe on long boards, the carriage lock and solid frame are real advantages, especially paired with well-adjusted infeed and outfeed support. It is a utilitarian machine without extras such as a second feed speed. Owners commonly mention that setting depth accurately takes a little practice and that dust collection should be connected for the best results. If you mostly plane long boards for tabletops and casework, it is a solid straight-knife choice.
**Pros:** Four-post carriage for stability; cutterhead lock; 13 in capacity; moderate cost.
**Cons:** Single feed speed; depth setting takes practice; basic features next to the DW735.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Delta+22-555+planer&tag=sktiger-20)

The RIDGID R4331 is a 13-inch, three-knife planer with a heavy base and a depth indicator that shows how much material the next pass will remove, which makes it easy to avoid overloading the motor. A carriage lock limits snipe and a dust port connects to collection.

Like many RIDGID tools, it is often covered by RIDGID's lifetime service agreement when registered, so check the current terms when you buy. The design is simple and sturdy rather than refined, and it lacks the DW735's two-speed gearbox and chip ejection fan. Availability varies by region and season. When you find it close to the DW734's price, it is a capable alternative, particularly if you value the cut-depth readout and RIDGID's service terms.
**Pros:** Depth indicator shows material removed per pass; carriage lock; sturdy base; RIDGID service terms when registered.
**Cons:** Availability varies; single feed speed; no chip ejection fan.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=RIDGID+R4331+planer&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: Which Planer Is Better, Knives or Helical?

blocks.p: Straight knives are better for low cost and straight-grained wood; helical heads are better for figured grain, reclaimed lumber and quieter running.

Two or three long knives span the full width. On pine, poplar, oak and maple they cut cleanly, the machines cost less, and double-sided disposable knives make upkeep easy. On figured or interlocked grain, a full-width knife can lift fibers ahead of the cut and cause tear-out. A nick in one knife leaves a raised line on every board until you shift or replace the knives.

Many small square inserts sit in a spiral. Each takes a shearing cut, which generally reduces tear-out and noise. A damaged insert gets rotated to a fresh edge, so a buried staple costs one insert. Carbide inserts last much longer than high-speed steel.

blocks.p: Helical heads can leave a faint scalloped pattern under raking light, and straight knives leave small ripples whose spacing depends on cuts per inch. Neither is a finished surface for fine furniture; plan on light sanding or scraping either way. Many woodworkers start with a DW735 and later fit an aftermarket helical head.

sections.h: DEWALT DW735 vs Other Planers: Which Is Second Best?

blocks.p: Next to the DW735X, the WEN PL1326 is the most common runner-up recommendation for value, and the Makita 2012NB for quiet operation. Which one is second best depends on what you would give up.

blocks.h3: If you want a helical head

blocks.p: The WEN PL1326 and Cutech 40200H-CT bring spiral cutterheads to benchtop prices. You trade the DW735's second feed speed and chip ejection fan for better results on difficult grain and easier insert replacement.
The Makita 2012NB lists about 83 decibels and adds automatic head clamping. You give up an inch of width and the DW735's finishing speed.

blocks.h3: If you want the DeWalt name for less

blocks.p: The DW734 shares DeWalt's knives and parts support and drops the second speed and ejection fan. For a few boards a month, the difference is small.

Buyers often compare the DW735 with Jet's 13-inch benchtop planers, including helical-head versions. Jet is not ranked in this list, so pull up Jet's current spec sheet and compare on the same points: width and thickness capacity, number of feed speeds, cuts per inch, snipe control and, on helical models, insert count and material.

blocks.h3: Cuts per inch and depth of cut

blocks.p: Higher cuts per inch give smaller knife marks. Two-speed planers let you choose a fast, low-CPI feed for dimensioning and a slow, high-CPI feed for the last pass. Maximum depth of cut is often listed at 1/8 inch on narrow boards and less at full width; treat it as a limit, not a target.

sections.h: How Do You Stop Planer Snipe?

blocks.p: Support the board level as it enters and leaves, feed boards end to end, use the head lock, and leave parts long so you can trim the sniped ends off.

Snipe is a slightly deeper cut, often a few thousandths of an inch, at the start or end of a board. It happens when only one feed roller holds the board, letting it tilt into the cutterhead, or when the carriage shifts. Every benchtop planer does it to some degree without good technique.

Set the infeed and outfeed tables level with, or a hair above, the bed. Support long boards on roller stands. Lift the trailing end slightly as the board enters and the leading end as it exits. Feed boards end to end so each one pushes the last through, or run a sacrificial board of the same thickness behind the final workpiece.

If snipe persists, make sure the bed and tables are clean and waxed with a silicone-free paste wax, the feed rollers are not glazed with pitch, and the carriage is not loose. Most manuals include a table and carriage adjustment procedure.
Cut parts a few inches over finished length before planing, then trim the ends afterward. It costs a little lumber and solves the problem entirely.

sections.h: Can a Planer Flatten a Board? Milling Rough Lumber

blocks.p: No. A thickness planer makes faces parallel; it does not flatten a cupped, bowed or twisted board. The feed rollers press the board flat as it passes under the knives, and once it leaves, the wood springs back to its old shape, only thinner.

Flatten one face on a jointer, square one edge to it, plane the opposite face parallel, then rip the second edge on the table saw. A planer alone is enough only if you buy lumber that is already surfaced and reasonably flat.

blocks.h3: Without a jointer: the planer sled

blocks.p: Set the board on a flat sheet of plywood or MDF, shim its high spots and fix it with hot glue or wedges so it cannot rock. Run sled and board through together to flatten the top face, then remove the board, flip it and plane the second face directly on the bed. This is how many hobbyists use a planer as a board flattener.

Indoor furniture lumber is commonly milled at roughly 6 to 8 percent moisture content in much of the US. Let boards acclimate in the shop for a week or two, check with a moisture meter, and rough-cut parts slightly oversize before milling. Remove wood equally from both faces and let boards rest overnight before the final pass, since internal stress can move them. Small defects that survive milling can be filled later; our [wood filler guide](/best-wood-filler/) covers fillers that take stain.

Feed with the grain so the cut does not lift fibers; if you see tear-out, flip the board end for end. Never feed pieces shorter than the manual's minimum, often 12 to 14 inches. Scan reclaimed wood for metal and brush off grit first.

sections.h: Do You Need Dust Collection for a Benchtop Planer?

blocks.p: Yes. A planer makes more chips per minute than almost any other home shop tool, and without collection the chips jam the chute, get pressed into the board as dents and cover the floor.

A dust collector with a 4-inch hose is ideal. For occasional use, a shop vac with a 2.5-inch hose can keep up if you put a cyclone separator between the planer and the vac so the filter does not clog. Our [shop vac picks](/best-shop-vac/) cover models with the airflow to keep up.

Benchtop planers are loud enough that hearing protection is necessary every session, even with the quieter models. Wear eye protection too, since chips and knot fragments can fly from the infeed. A respirator helps for long sessions, especially with western red cedar and some exotics that irritate airways.

Most benchtop planers draw up to 15 amps under load. Run one on a circuit with nothing else drawing power, ideally 20 amps, and avoid long extension cords. A planer and a large vac on one 15-amp circuit can trip the breaker. For choosing a battery platform for the rest of the shop, see [Milwaukee vs DeWalt](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/).

sections.h: How Do You Set Up and Maintain a Benchtop Planer?

blocks.p: Put it on a rigid stand with runway on both sides, check it against calipers before the first board, and keep knives sharp and rollers clean.

A planer that must be hauled from under the bench gets used less than one on a mobile stand at working height. Flip-top carts are popular in small garages. The stand must be rigid, because a rocking base causes snipe no adjustment can fix. Allow clear space in front and behind of at least the longest board's length; an 8-foot board needs roughly 16 feet of runway.

Confirm the tables are level with the bed using a straightedge. Plane a test board and measure both edges with calipers; a difference means the head is out of parallel with the bed. Compare the depth scale with the calipers and note any offset. Pencil a scribble across each face before a pass; when it disappears, the whole face has been cut.

When one edge of a double-sided knife dulls, flip it; when both are dull, replace the set. Fuzzy surfaces, more tear-out, a laboring motor and slower feeding all signal dull knives. A single nick can be hidden by shifting one knife slightly sideways. On helical heads, rotate the damaged insert and keep the seat spotless, since a speck of debris under an insert leaves a line.
Clean pitch off the feed rollers with resin remover or mineral spirits, unplugged. Wax the bed. Check belts, chains and gears per the manual, and always unplug the planer before reaching inside.

mistakes: Expecting the planer to flatten a warped board

Rollers press a cupped or twisted board flat while it is cut, and it springs back as it leaves, so you get a thinner board with the same warp. Create a flat reference face first with a jointer, a planer sled or a hand plane, then use the planer to make the other face parallel.

Cutting the full listed depth every pass bogs the motor, increases tear-out and snipe, and wears knives faster. Passes of 1/32 to 1/16 inch leave a better surface and are rarely slower overall. Use the depth gauge if your planer has one, and save deeper cuts for narrow boards.
Cutting parts to final length before planing

Snipe lands at the ends of boards, so parts already at final length carry it into the finished piece. Leave parts a few inches long, plane them, then trim the ends. It costs a little lumber and saves sanding out every sniped end by hand.
Planing reclaimed wood without a metal check

Old nails, staples, screws and embedded grit chip knives, damage helical inserts and can throw fragments. Sweep reclaimed boards with a metal detector, pull anything you find and brush off dirt. Check again after each pass, because buried metal can surface as wood comes off.

Chips that are not pulled away get pressed back into the board as dents, clog the chute and spread across the shop. Hook up a dust collector or a wide-hose shop vac with a cyclone separator before the first board. Surfaces come out cleaner and cleanup takes minutes.
bottomLine: For most home shops, the best benchtop planer is the DEWALT DW735X, thanks to its two feed speeds, 13-inch capacity, chip ejection and included tables. Choose the Makita 2012NB when noise matters, the WEN PL1326 or Cutech 40200H-CT for a helical head on figured or reclaimed wood, the DEWALT DW734 for occasional use, and the Delta 22-555 if snipe on long boards is your main frustration. Whichever you buy, remember what a planer does: it makes faces parallel. Give it a flat reference face, feed with the grain, take light passes, leave parts long and connect dust collection before the first board.

faqs.q: What is the best benchtop planer for woodworking?
faqs.a: The DEWALT DW735X is the best benchtop planer for most woodworkers, with 13-inch width and 6-inch thickness capacity, two feed speeds and included infeed and outfeed tables. Choose the Makita 2012NB if noise is a concern, and the WEN PL1326 if you want a helical head for figured or reclaimed wood without a large outlay.

faqs.q: What is the best benchtop helical planer?
faqs.a: For value, the WEN PL1326 is the strongest helical pick here, with a 13-inch spiral head of indexable inserts at a price close to straight-knife machines. The Cutech 40200H-CT is a lighter alternative for shops that move the planer often. Check insert material when you buy, since carbide inserts last much longer between rotations.

faqs.q: Are helical cutterheads worth the extra cost?
faqs.a: Yes for figured, curly or interlocked grain and for reclaimed lumber, because helical heads generally reduce tear-out, run quieter and let you rotate a single damaged insert. For straight-grained pine, poplar, oak and maple, a sharp straight-knife head works well and costs less to buy and maintain.

faqs.q: How deep should each planer pass be?
faqs.a: Most woodworkers take passes of about 1/32 to 1/16 inch, especially on wide boards and near final thickness. Manufacturers often list a maximum of 1/8 inch on narrow boards, but heavy cuts strain the motor and increase tear-out and snipe. Several light passes usually give a better surface in about the same time.

faqs.q: Can I use a shop vac for planer dust collection?
faqs.a: Yes for occasional use, with a 2.5-inch hose and a cyclone separator between the planer and the vac. Without the separator, the filter clogs and the tank fills fast. For regular milling sessions, a dust collector with a 4-inch hose handles the chip volume better and keeps the planer from jamming.

faqs.q: Do I need a jointer if I own a planer?
faqs.a: Not strictly. If you buy surfaced lumber that is reasonably flat, a planer alone brings it to thickness. For rough lumber you need a flat face and straight edge first. A jointer is fastest, but a planer sled for faces and a table saw jig for edges work well for occasional milling.

faqs.q: How do I stop snipe on a benchtop planer?
faqs.a: Level the infeed and outfeed tables with the bed, support long boards, lift the board ends slightly as they enter and leave, feed boards end to end and use the head lock if your planer has one. The surest fix is leaving parts a few inches long and trimming the sniped ends after planing.
